title: The rains retreat
hookLine: for three months of monsoon monks stay in one place; lay people take on a practice
last: MAGHA PUJA — THEY CAME WITHOUT BEING CALLED.

cards: July in northeast Thailand. The monsoon has arrived. The roads are mud, the rice fields flooded and green, and in the city of Ubon, people are carving huge wax candles and parading them through the streets to the temples.
The candles are meant to burn a long time, because the monks are about to stop traveling. For the next three months they will stay put.
And in many homes, people are quietly deciding what they will give up, or take on, until the rains end.

teach.h: VASSA — RAIN, THEN THE RAINY SEASON.
teach.b: The Pali word is vassa: rain, and then the rainy season. In the Buddha's time, wandering was the monk's life: walk from village to village, sleep under trees, take alms, move on.
The monastic rulebook, the Vinaya, tells how that changed.

People complained that the wandering monks were tramping through the young green crops in the wet season and crushing small living things underfoot. Even other wandering groups, they said, stopped for the rains.
So the Buddha allowed the monks to settle in one place for the three months of the monsoon. A practical rule about mud and seedlings became the heart of the monastic year.
The retreat begins the day after the Asalha full moon, usually in July, and ends three lunar months later at a full moon, usually in October.

teach.h: MONKS COUNT THEIR YEARS IN RAINS.
teach.b: Monks still count their seniority in rains: a monk of ten rains has kept ten retreats. The last day has a custom called pavarana, the invitation.
Each monk invites the others to tell him anything he did wrong during the season, seen, heard or suspected: three months together, then an open door for honest correction.

teach.h: LAY PEOPLE TAKE ON ONE PRACTICE.
teach.b: Lay people join in their own way. Some choose one practice for the whole season: no alcohol, the eight precepts on every moon day, a daily sitting, a morning at the temple.
In Thailand, some young men ordain as monks for just these three months. The point is the same for both. Stop wandering.
Stay in one place long enough for something to take root.

how: In Theravada countries monks stay in one monastery for the three months of the rainy season, roughly July to October, and some lay people take on an extra practice for the season, such as giving up alcohol or keeping the eight precepts on moon days.

practice: Think about the next three months, one full season, the length of the rains, and let a few possible practices come to mind: a short sitting every morning, no phone in bed, the five precepts kept a little more carefully, one kind act a day.
Don't choose the most heroic one; choose the one you could actually keep through the rain, the boredom and the busy weeks. When you've got it, hold it quietly and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Vassa. Rain, and the three-month retreat of the rainy season, when monks stop wandering and stay in one place.

orig.note: Pali: rain, the rainy season, and the retreat kept through it.
